title: GenRecs Tokenization: Transforming Ads Recommendation at Meta with Stable Model Vocabulary
abstract: Generative Recommenders (GenRecs) represent a paradigm shift from scoring every ad to reasoning about ad content and user preferences together in order to predict the best outcome for advertisers. Leveraging the world knowledge built into LLMs makes ad matching more intelligent and precise, compounding gains for advertisers. GenRecs Tokenization is the foundational data representation that makes this possible. Rather than maintaining a dedicated ID for every item, GenRecs Tokenization represents each item with a set of tokens from a stable semantic vocabulary. Paired with Meta’s Generative Ads Model (GEM) and Meta’s Adaptive Ranking Model , GenRecs Tokenization has delivered a +0.35% lift in conversions across surfaces for advertisers. GenRecs improves the way Meta’s ads recommendation systems make predictions today. Short for Generative Recommenders , GenRecs shifts our approach from scoring every individual ad candidate to leveraging LLM architecture to deeply reason about ad content and user preferences simultaneously. By pairing pre-trained world knowledge with a semantic understanding of what an ad actually represents, the system moves beyond click-pattern matching to understand underlying user preferences. This allows the model to predict the most relevant ad for each person, even when surfacing brand-new products with no past product, ad or company engagement history. GenRecs Tokenization is the foundational data representation that makes this possible. Instead of maintaining a dedicated ID for every concept in the world, language models compose a small vocabulary of semantic tokens to represent any concept. Because tokens describe what an item (e.g., ads, products, services, etc.) is, the model can relate an item it has never seen engagement for, to items it knows well. A newly launched “trail shoe” inherits what the model has already learned about that category, rather than starting a new representation with no signal. GenRecs Tokenization introduces a structured vocabulary approach for ad recommendations, enabling GenRecs for both retrieval and ranking across every item type in the system, including ads, products, pages, and pixels. Meta’s state-of-the-art ads recommendation system drives ongoing advertiser performance improvements by learning about individual items and how they perform . LLMs present a unique opportunity to further improve the performance of recommendation systems by leveraging semantic tokenization in several ads use cases: Accelerating learning from new entities: Semantic tokenization helps models to infer relevance and establish relationships through shared concepts. New entities include newly created ads, niche products, and pages with limited engagement. Enabling cross-campaign transfer: Semantic tokenization creates a stable vocabulary that allows the models to carry insights across campaigns for advertisers. LLM scaling benefits: Semantic tokenization allows the benefits to compound with the LLM scaling curve’s improving performance. Infusing world knowledge: Semantic tokenization gives pre-trained language models a direct interface to reason about ad content and user intent. Once items are migrated to semantic tokens, models learn from token patterns much like LLMs do. In production, this yields: Prediction accuracy improvements in production: Paired with Meta’s GEM and Adaptive Ranking Model , GenRecs Tokenization delivered a +0.35% lift 1 in conversions. Compounding feedback loop: Better tail predictions yield better lessons from tail ads which enrich the training data to further improve predictions for all ads from the model, creating a performance improving feedback loop. A new way to scale: Across production ranking and retrieval, tokens bend the scaling curve along sequence length, training data, and model architecture. 1 Meta Internal Data, measured in February 2026. title: The Thin Orchestrator: How We Made Our AI Agents More Reliable by Giving the Router Less to Do
abstract: Sometimes, giving an AI agent all of the knowledge it needs is the wrong approach. At Meta, we’ve seen notable improvements in efficiency and accuracy by keeping the orchestration layer of our data pipeline agents deliberately thin: It routes work and enforces reliability checks, while specialized agents do the domain reasoning. We’re sharing our own process and insights, plus how any team can apply this to their production AI agents. We built a 1,300-line orchestrator that routes 20+ workflows to 14 specialized AI agents. It performs zero domain work itself. That’s the point. When we first deployed AI agents to automate data column onboarding across Meta’s recommendation systems — a process spanning three code repositories, three programming languages, and up to six pipeline stages that must stay in sync — we did what most teams do: We built one smart agent that knew everything. It worked in demos. In production, it started hallucinating. The fix wasn’t better prompts or a bigger context window. It was giving the central agent less to do. We call this the thin orchestrator pattern: a router that owns sequencing and reliability checks, and leaves every domain decision to specialists. The Problem: More Context, Worse Results Our pipeline is config-as-code: Python configurations drive C++ code generation, which feeds data processing services, which populate analytics systems. Onboarding a single data column requires coordinated changes across configuration registries, backend services, and data pipelines, and each column moves through up to six stages before its data arrives. Our first approach was a single AI agent loaded with all domain knowledge, configuration schemas, code generation rules, pipeline routing logic, validation requirements, and population patterns for 10+ data sources. The agent had everything it needed. That was the problem. Past a certain context threshold, additional knowledge degraded rather than improved performance. The agent would cross-contaminate concepts, applying field naming conventions from one subsystem to another, or using a code generation pattern meant for one data source when populating from a different one. A preprint from the Windreich Department of Artificial Intelligence and Human Health at Mount Sinai found that orchestrated multiagent systems held 65.3% accuracy at 80-task batches where single agents fell to 16.6%, while reducing token usage up to 65-fold. The authors attribute this to the design’s isolation of tasks, which prevented context interference. We were experiencing the inverse, a single agent drowning in its own knowledge. We also evaluated an alternative single-agent approach. Its success rate was 70-80% with manual prompt engineering per task: An engineer had to craft a custom system prompt for each specific job. Without that handholding, success dropped to 10-20%. This wasn’t a prompt engineering problem. It was an architectural one. The Approach: A Thin Router With Specialist Workers We split the system into two layers: A deterministic orchestrator that performs zero domain work. It classifies intent, gathers required fields, runs reliability checks, and delegates to the right specialist. It never reasons about code, never generates configurations, and never touches the codebase. It’s a router. Fourteen specialized subagents , each a complete domain expert with isolated context. A schema management agent knows configuration registries. A population agent knows how to generate code for each of 10 data sources. A validation agent knows build systems and quality checks. No agent sees the full picture. That’s the feature, not the bug. The orchestrator follows a fixed 7-step protocol for every request: Read the relevant subagent’s instruction file. Check if the target already exists (prevent duplicates). Gather required fields from the user. Auto-discover what can be inferred (repository type, existing configurations). title: Inside Prometheus: Meta’s Journey to a Gigawatt-Scale Supercluster
abstract: With the recent release of the Muse family of foundational models, we want to take you inside the infrastructure that has made it all possible. The first phase of Prometheus, our gigawatt-scale supercluster, is already complete and we’re working toward scaling it to comprise ~1 million GPUs. Prometheus also features technologies like closed-loop liquid cooling to help it operate efficiently. Right now, in New Albany, Ohio, Meta is undertaking its most ambitious AI infrastructure project to date. Prometheus, our gigawatt-scale supercluster, is an advancement in our infrastructure that is training the next generation of foundational models that will bring new AI experiences to billions of people. Two years ago, New Albany was a conventional data center site running web traffic. With advancements in hardware, networking and building design, we reworked this site to be home to training programs for frontier models. We’re building the supercluster in phases. The first phase has already been completed and was used to train our Muse foundational models , including the Muse Wonder models, our new frontier models that deliver state-of-the-art performance on personal and professional agentic tasks. Large training jobs require everything to work optimally to sustain their performance; an issue on a single host can slow down or stop the entire job, lowering its ‘goodput’. By focusing on improving our systems’ stability and reliability we were able to achieve more than 85% goodput for pre-training runs and more than 90% goodput for reinforcement learning (RL) runs of Muse Wonder. During these training runs, we were able to achieve an overall wall-clock mean time between interruptions (MTBI) of ~47k GPU hours. Since then, we have landed further changes across our fleet including firmware fixes to increase MTBI to more than 54K GPU hours, and we are constantly improving it. Now, we’re continuing to scale Prometheus with our next frontier models from Meta Superintelligence Labs in mind. https://engineering.fb.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/AIM-1210-Superclusters_Video_v1.mp4 The Prometheus supercluster is housed in Meta’s New Albany, Ohio, data center. The Supercluster: Unlocking New AI Capabilities Today, Prometheus comprises an array of hundreds of thousands of GPUs across multiple interconnected buildings, including traditional and AI-optimized data center buildings and rapid deployment structures, all tightly interconnected by miles of fiber and functioning as a single machine. This capacity allows us to pursue larger models and longer context windows than were previously practical. At full scale, Prometheus will comprise roughly 1 million distributed GPUs, all functioning in lockstep. Multiple Generations of AI Hardware Prometheus currently deploys two NVIDIA GPU platforms, with a third (based on NVIDIA’s Vera Rubin NVL72 ) arriving soon. Each represents a generational leap in performance and efficiency, leveraging our NVL72 rack architecture where 72 GPUs act as a single accelerator within the same network fabric. Catalina: NVIDIA GB200 Our first platform, Catalina , leverages the NVIDIA GB200 NVL72. We deploy the Ariel variant, a two-rack configuration in which 36 GPUs per rack are interconnected via NVLink to form a unified 72-GPU domain. Catalina provides improvements in raw compute and memory capacity compared to Grand Teton H100 . It leverages our Open Rack V3 (ORv3) high-power rack (HPR) structure, an open hardware design contributed to the Open Compute Project (OCP) . The Ariel variant of GB200 NVL72 pairs each NVIDIA Blackwell GPU with an NVIDIA Grace CPU and 2x NVIDIA ConnectX-7 400G NICs at a 1:1 CPU-to-GPU ratio, letting us deploy 800G of I/O per GPU earlier than the rest of the industry. title: Structured outputs for Anthropic Claude models on Amazon Bedrock
abstract: Amazon Bedrock now supports structured outputs for all Anthropic Claude models, on both the bedrock-runtime and bedrock-mantle endpoints, where the model is available. Whether you call Claude through Boto3 and the bedrock-runtime APIs or through the Messages API and the bedrock-mantle endpoint, you can now receive schema-compliant JSON responses that conform to a defined structure. You no longer need custom parsing, retry logic, or post-processing. Practical applications With structured outputs for Claude on Amazon Bedrock, you can automate reliable, schema-compliant tasks across industries. Examples include extracting every required field from financial earnings reports and compliance documents, parsing clinical notes into Electronic Health Records (EHR), and enriching product catalogs with consistent, validated results. You can also analyze contracts for key terms, parties, and obligations, or power intelligent support ticket routing where intents, sentiments, and entities always match your application’s data model. What changes with structured outputs on Amazon Bedrock Structured outputs use constrained decoding to enforce your JSON schema during token generation, not after the fact. The model doesn’t produce tokens that would violate your schema. This changes output formatting from probabilistic to deterministic. Two complementary mechanisms are now available on both Amazon Bedrock endpoints: Feature Purpose Use case JSON Schema output format Control the model’s response structure Data extraction, report generation, API responses Strict tool use Validate tool parameters against schemas Agentic workflows, function calling, multi-step automation What this means for you Each response is a valid JSON, so you no longer encounter JSON.parse() errors or parsing exceptions. Responses are also type safe: field types are enforced, and required fields are always present. Because outputs always conform to your schema, you don’t need retries to handle schema violations, making your integration more reliable. Structured outputs also constrains responses to only the fields your schema defines, which reduces output token count and can lower inference costs for high-volume workloads. These properties make structured outputs production ready, so you can deploy at scale without additional schema-validation code. Supported models and availability Structured outputs works with batch inference , so you can process large volumes of requests asynchronously while still receiving schema-compliant outputs. On the bedrock-runtime endpoint, it also works with cross-Region inference, so you can use it across AWS Regions without additional setup. If you need responses in real time, you can stream structured responses as typed events. How it works When you make a request with a JSON schema, here’s what happens behind the scenes: Schema validation – Amazon Bedrock validates your JSON schema against the supported JSON Schema Draft 2020-12 subset. Grammar compilation – For new schemas, Amazon Bedrock compiles a grammar artifact (the first request might take slightly longer). Caching – Compiled grammars are cached for 24 hours, making subsequent requests faster. Constrained generation – The model generates tokens that produce valid JSON matching your schema. Performance considerations For performance, the first request with a new schema might take longer because Amazon Bedrock compiles a grammar artifact before generation begins. After that initial compilation, subsequent requests using the same schema run with minimal overhead because the compiled grammar is cached. This cache is scoped to your account and lasts for 24 hours from first access. Changing the structure of your JSON schema invalidates the cache and triggers a fresh compilation, while changing only the name or description fields leaves the cached grammar intact. title: Developers can now access SageMaker Studio through the new AWS experience
abstract: Today, we’re excited to announce that new Amazon SageMaker AI customers can now land inside a fully configured Amazon SageMaker Studio environment in only a few steps after signing up for AWS. You can use a sign-in method that you already have, such as Amazon, Apple, GitHub, Google, or an email address. You don’t need to set up an advanced AWS account, enter a credit card (for most customers), or configure an environment manually. New customers also receive $100 in AWS Free Tier credits that work across SageMaker AI, including model customization, training jobs, Studio notebooks, and endpoint deployments. This post follows on from our previous post, From Hugging Face to Amazon SageMaker Studio in One Click , which introduced deep links from Hugging Face model pages directly into SageMaker Studio workflows. Earlier this year, we also sped up Studio environment creation time from 2 minutes to about 20 seconds and pre-configured model customization permissions in every new Studio domain. Together, these changes removed much of the friction after a developer reached Studio. One major hurdle remained before they got there: creating an AWS account. New customers had to verify an email address, enter contact information, verify a phone number, provide payment details, and select a support plan before they could start building. For individual developers and small startup teams used to signing in and building within a few minutes, that was still a significant barrier. What’s new With this launch, SageMaker Studio is now integrated with the updated AWS sign-in and sign-up experience , which introduces new options for creating and managing AWS accounts along with simplified collaboration. New customers can create an account using an identity that they already have and start building in SageMaker Studio right away. title: Amazon SageMaker JumpStart: 2026 year-to-date in review
abstract: Amazon SageMaker JumpStart is a machine learning (ML) hub within Amazon SageMaker AI that provides access to a curated catalog of AI models, solution templates, and example notebooks. It reduces the time it takes to go from model selection to deployment. You can use it to evaluate open source large language models (LLMs), deploy a vision model for document understanding, or fine-tune a compact model on your own data. SageMaker JumpStart serves three primary use cases: Model discovery and evaluation — Browse hundreds of foundation models (FMs) from providers like Alibaba (Qwen), NVIDIA, Google, Mistral, Cohere, IBM, and more. Each model card includes architecture details, benchmarks, licensing information, and sample notebooks. One-click deployment — Deploy your choice of model to a SageMaker real-time inference endpoint with pre-configured settings optimized for your workload (low cost, low latency, throughput, or balanced). No manual container or instance configuration required. Model customization — Fine-tune models directly from the console or SDK using techniques like low-rank adaptation (LoRA), supervised fine-tuning (SFT), direct preference optimization (DPO), and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). Serverless customization options reduce infrastructure management. You can access SageMaker JumpStart through the SageMaker Studio console (Models → JumpStart models), programmatically through the SageMaker Python SDK, or directly from Hugging Face using the recently launched deep link integration. 2026 onboarding at a glance From January through September 2026, SageMaker JumpStart onboarded over 100 new models across 30 distinct providers. title: Pegasus 1.5 from TwelveLabs is now available in Amazon Bedrock
abstract: On Oct 9, 2026 we announced the availability of TwelveLabs’ Pegasus 1.5 on Amazon Bedrock . Pegasus 1.5 is a video language model that turns long-form video into structured, timestamped metadata. You describe the moments that matter to your workflow, and the model returns every matching segment as JSON. Video represents a significant and complex category of unstructured data, yet most of it remains unsearchable and underutilized. Extracting structured, actionable insights from that content has historically required labor-intensive manual review or fragmented toolchains. With earlier versions of Pegasus, you can point the model at a clip, ask a question, and get an answer. Now, Pegasus 1.5 analyzes the entire video, finds every segment that matches user-defined criteria, and returns structured, timestamped metadata. It also introduces video segmentation, multimodal prompting with reference images, and on-the-fly processing. With Pegasus 1.5 on Amazon Bedrock, you can analyze videos directly from an Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) URI or a base64 string with no pre-indexing required, and your data remains within the AWS data boundary. In this post, we cover what’s new in Pegasus 1.5, how the model is packaged on Amazon Bedrock, and how to send your first request. We then walk through video segmentation, structured JSON output, and multimodal prompting. What’s new in Pegasus 1.5 Pegasus 1.5 has the following changes compared to previous versions: Time-based metadata generation. You define the segments, events, or domain-specific cues that matter to your workflow, such as editorial segments, sports plays, speaker changes, or brand appearances. Pegasus 1.5 returns every matching segment as JSON, with start and end times and the requested fields populated. Multimodal prompting. A segment definition can combine a text description with a visual reference. This makes it possible to locate a specific product, logo, or person, along with what they are doing on screen. On-the-fly processing. No ingestion pipeline or pre-indexing step is required. Videos are sent directly from Amazon S3 and results are returned in the response. Extended processing capacity. Pegasus 1.5 analyzes videos up to two hours long in a single request, up from one hour in Pegasus 1.2. Pegasus 1.5 retains and enhances the core capabilities that made Pegasus 1.2 a powerful tool for video understanding, including: Video-to-text generation : Creates detailed textual descriptions based on video content. Granular visual comprehension : Analyzes objects, on-screen text, and numerical content within video frames. Temporal grounding : Accurately identifies timestamps of specific events within videos. Multimodal understanding : Combines visual, audio, and textual information for comprehensive analysis. Multilingual support : Full support for English, with partial support for Arabic, Chinese, French, German, Italian, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, Russian, Spanish, Thai, and Vietnamese. How Pegasus 1.5 works on Amazon Bedrock Pegasus 1.5 takes a video and either a text prompt or a set of segment definitions, and returns text or JSON. You call it on the bedrock-runtime endpoint with the InvokeModel API, or with InvokeModelWithResponseStream when you want the response streamed as it’s generated. title: How Deepgram optimized voice AI at scale with AWS Trainium
abstract: As voice becomes a first-class modality for AI, Deepgram’s models span speech-to-text, text-to-speech, and voice agents. They now process quadrillions of audio tokens a year for more than 200,000 developers and 1,400 organizations. Customers use them through the Deepgram API or run them in their own environments, including on Amazon SageMaker AI. For Deepgram, serving efficiency determines how much audio the system can process for a given infrastructure budget. High-volume batch workloads put heavy pressure on that budget, so the more efficiently each accelerator hour is used, the more audio Deepgram can serve on the same fleet. That made inference efficiency a natural target and Deepgram turned to AWS AI chips to improve it. They worked with AWS to bring its Nova-3 speech-to-text model to AWS Trainium2 for offline batch workloads such as contact-center analytics and medical transcription. The engagement began with Deepgram delivering Nova-3 as standard PyTorch code. Over several months, Deepgram and the AWS Forward Deployed Engineering (FDE) team ported Nova-3 to AWS Trainium2 in PyTorch reconstruction and tuned it for the new hardware. The final configuration runs eight model replicas on a single Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) trn2.3xlarge instance. On Deepgram’s offline, throughput-oriented batch workloads, that setup processed 11–70 percent more audio per dollar than the compute options Deepgram had been running. We measured this using instance pricing at the time of the evaluation. These gains help Deepgram scale efficiently, keep shipping better models, and bring them to customers at lower prices. These benefits can extend to customers who self-host Deepgram models in their own virtual private cloud (VPC) on Amazon SageMaker AI. There, Deepgram and AWS continue to improve ease of setup, reliability, and observability. In this post, we walk through the full inference optimization effort on Trainium: porting Nova-3 to the AWS Neuron software stack, the kernel-level tuning that followed, the data-parallel Rust runtime that lets Deepgram’s own model server call Trainium, and the throughput and cost results we measured on batch transcription. Optimizing Nova-3 to Trainium2 with native PyTorch Starting with standard PyTorch code, we used TorchNeuron, the native PyTorch integration of the Neuron Compiler, which supports both eager execution and torch.compile . We ran Nova-3 in eager mode on Trainium2 first and checked which operations fell back to the CPU, then compiled with torch.compile . The compiled path ran every model operation on Trainium2 with no CPU fallbacks detected. We compiled the encoder and decoder as separate static-shape graphs using torch.compile . Throughout, we checked numerical accuracy at two levels: layer-level output consistency against CPU, and the end-to-end Word Error Rate (WER), which had to stay in line with Deepgram’s reference values and target. From that working baseline, we kicked off the optimization work by replacing several layers with fused kernels from the public NKI Library (NKILib), a collection of pre-built reference kernels written with the Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI). The kernels covered operations such as fused QKV projections, fused feed-forward network (FFN) layers, and depthwise 1D convolution. We optimized for throughput and, by extension, cost efficiency, targeting Deepgram’s offline inference workloads. Throughput is reported as a relative gain over a baseline configuration rather than as absolute audio processed per second, and we swept batch sizes 1–128 to find the throughput-maximizing batch size. title: Push-based KV transfer to improve TTFT and TPOT for disaggregated inference in vLLM
abstract: vLLM is an open-source inference and serving engine for large language models (LLMs). LLM inference has two distinct phases: prefill, which processes the input prompt and builds the key-value (KV) cache, and decode, which uses that cache to generate output one token at a time. These phases have different compute, memory, and scaling characteristics. Prefill-decode (P-D) disaggregation runs them on separate engine instances, allowing each phase to scale and be optimized independently. This can improve resource utilization, throughput, and latency under load. However, it also requires transferring the KV cache from the prefill instance to the decode instance before token generation can begin, making efficient KV transfer critical to time-to-first-token (TTFT). One of the ways vLLM performs this transfer is through the NVIDIA Inference Xfer Library (NIXL) connector , which moves KV blocks over interconnects that support Remote Direct Memory Access (RDMA), such as AWS Elastic Fabric Adapter ( AWS EFA , the low-latency RDMA network used across servers in AWS). On supported instance types , AWS EFA supports GPUDirect RDMA and Neuron Direct RDMA. NIXL can therefore transfer KV blocks directly between GPU or AWS Trainium device memory without staging through host memory. The default mode for NIXL connector is pull-based : After the prefill instance finishes computing the prompt KV cache, the router relays the source metadata, including the prefill block IDs, to the decode instance. The decode instance then allocates destination blocks, prepares the NIXL transfer, and initiates NIXL READ to pull the KV blocks from the prefill instance. Because these coordination and setup steps occur sequentially after prefill and before decoding can begin, they extend the TTFT critical path, as shown in the following timeline. Figure 1: Pull-mode KV transfer timeline, where the router relay, decode-side allocation, and NIXL READ run serially on the path to the first token This post introduces a push-based NIXL connector that moves post-prefill transfer coordination and setup off the critical path. If you run disaggregated prefill/decode inference with vLLM, push mode can improve application responsiveness by reducing TTFT and TPOT, particularly at high request rates. In our benchmark on a 1P1D deployment using Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) P5en instances connected with EFA, push mode delivered up to 3x better TTFT and up to 30 percent better time-per-output-token (TPOT) compared to pull mode (see the Performance data section) for the Qwen3-32B model. Results depend on workload and configuration. We built and validated the feature on AWS Trainium instance clusters connected with EFA, and then we contributed it to vLLM as an accelerator-agnostic feature. The results here are from an Amazon EC2 P5en (GPU) cluster with EFA, showing the gains carry over to GPUs. This post explains the push-based architecture, transfer flow, threading model, performance results, and how to reproduce the benchmark. Push-based KV transfer This section explains the push-based design: its architecture, the transfer protocol, and the threading model that keeps KV transfer off the critical path. Architecture overview Push-based transfer improves TTFT and decode throughput for two reasons: It removes the serialization of the pull model by overlapping producer and consumer work. The decode instance registers its target blocks in advance while the producer is still computing KV. The transfer then begins as soon as the producer’s blocks are ready, rather than after a consumer-side ID-discovery round trip, removing that round trip from the path to first token. title: Improve TTFT for multi-turn agentic workloads with bi-directional KV transfer in vLLM
abstract: Multi-turn agentic workloads build on accumulated context as an agent reasons, invokes tools, and incorporates earlier results. With each new turn, the client resends the conversation history, including system instructions, prior prompts, tool results, and model responses, causing the growing context to be processed repeatedly. In Prefill-decode (P-D) disaggregation , each request is split across specialized nodes: the prefill node processes the prompt and builds its key-value (KV) cache, then the decode node retrieves those KV blocks and generates the response. Conventional disaggregated serving, however, only transfers KV cache in one direction: from prefill to decode node. This one-directional flow creates two inefficiencies for multi-turn workloads. First, after generating a response, the decode node holds KV cache entries for both the prompt and the newly generated tokens. When processing the next turn, the prefill node cannot retrieve those entries, so it must recompute the KV projections for the previous response tokens. Second, the decode node maintains the session state while the prefill nodes don’t, increasing the probability of cache eviction for active sessions on the prefill nodes. On a full cache miss, the prefill node must recompute KV projections for the entire conversation history, including system instructions, prior user requests, tool results, and model-generated responses. As the conversation grows, this redundant work consumes more accelerator capacity and increases time to first token (TTFT). When you build conversational assistants and agentic applications, longer interaction histories can increase latency and consume accelerator capacity through repeated prefill computation. In this post, we show how bi-directional KV cache transfer lets prefill and decode nodes reuse previously computed context across turns, which improves accelerator utilization and helps applications sustain responsive TTFT as conversations grow. In our multi-turn benchmarks on a 1P1D deployment using Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) P5en instances, bi-directional KV transfer reduced TTFT by up to 1.6x for Qwen3-32B and up to 3.3x for zai-org/GLM-5-FP8 (see the Performance data section). Results vary with workload and configuration. The instances are connected with AWS Elastic Fabric Adapter ( AWS EFA ), a low-latency remote direct memory access (RDMA) network used across servers in AWS. On supported instance types , AWS EFA supports GPUDirect RDMA and Neuron Direct RDMA to move KV blocks directly between GPU or AWS Trainium device memory on the prefill and decode nodes. We originally built and validated the feature on AWS Trainium instance clusters connected with EFA and contributed it to vLLM as an accelerator-agnostic capability. The results presented here are from an Amazon EC2 P5en GPU cluster with EFA, showing that the benefits also carry over to GPUs. This post explains the bi-directional KV transfer architecture, router metadata flow, KV-block retention and recompute controls, performance results, and how to reproduce the benchmark. Bi-directional KV transfer Bi-directional KV transfer is a mechanism in which a decode node returns previously computed KV to a prefill node on subsequent turns of a conversation. This avoids recomputing shared context on the prefill node and is governed by a configurable KV recompute threshold. It mitigates both computational-redundancy scenarios described earlier. To make it work, the KV must survive past the turn that produced it and travel in the reverse direction, coordinated by a KV-cache-aware router. title: AI Changed How We Code. It Hasn’t Changed How We Work Together.
abstract: This summer, I built a small experiment called ContextCue . The idea came from something I kept seeing during my internship. The engineers around me were using AI everywhere in the software development process. GitHub Copilot and Claude models helped with specs, code, reviews, and tests. The team also maintained reusable skills that taught coding agents how the team worked. One of those skills could take a UI design and turn it into working frontend code. The code was moving faster, but the understanding around the code did not seem to move faster with it. The software was being built by nine teams spread across three continents, with one team working closely with the customer. A request might begin in a customer conversation, move through one team, then reach another team several time zones away. By the time the work reached engineering, some of the original meaning could be missing. That was the problem I wanted ContextCue to explore. ContextCue takes recorded meetings and tries to preserve more than a transcript or summary. It keeps the spoken discussion, important visual context from the screen, the decisions that were made, the reasons behind them, and the source they came from. The goal is to create a shared piece of context that can move with the work from one team to another. It is still an experiment, but the problem behind it felt very real. As far as I could see, a lot of time in distributed software teams went into reaching a common understanding before the coding even started. AI was already helping with the final stages of software development. I wanted to see whether it could help earlier, while teams were still trying to understand what they were building and why. Where the context disappears Meetings were already being recorded, and tools like Microsoft Teams could produce an AI summary. On my team, that summary often arrived as an email and stayed there. That worked well enough for the people who attended the meeting. It was less useful for the team that picked up the work later, especially if that team was in another country and had not seen the original conversation. There were two other problems. A summary usually covered one meeting, while the understanding behind a feature was often built across several. Different teams might discuss the same request days apart, each adding a new constraint or interpretation. A transcript could also miss important visual context. Many of our conversations involved screen sharing. Someone might point at a page and say, “This is too slow,” or highlight a part of a workflow while explaining what needed to change. The words alone did not always carry the meaning. That is where I started thinking about context as something larger than a transcript. A simple example Imagine that a customer asks for a “faster report.” During the call, the customer shares a screen, points at a page that is slow to open, and explains that managers use it every morning before a meeting. Everyone on that call understands that “faster” means the page should open more quickly. Two days later, another team in another time zone discusses the same request. Nobody in that meeting saw the original screen. They read “faster report” as “the report should finish running sooner” and begin planning backend work. Both meeting summaries might contain the same phrase: Make the report faster. Nothing in that sentence shows that the two teams mean different things. The problem only becomes visible when the customer sees the result. This is a simple example, but it captures the issue I kept noticing. Requirements move through people before they ever become code. If the meaning changes during that process, AI can help a team implement the wrong interpretation very efficiently. title: Making the internet better for AI agents might make it worse for everyone else
abstract: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here . Until recently, you could divide internet users into just two categories: bots and people. Websites have long allowed bots to perform automated tasks, like capturing the content of web pages, but rules govern what they can access and how they behave. The web, after all, is designed primarily for people, even if we occasionally have to solve puzzles and captchas to prove we are not bots. But this is being entirely upended by the release of personal AI agents, which can do things for you online, like booking flights or hotel rooms. They have recently been unleashed at scale by the launch of apps like OpenAI’s Dots and Meta’s Muse. Muse was downloaded 5 million times in its first month, and agentic web traffic tripled from August to September. The mingling of these agents with human visitors—on an internet designed largely to prioritize people—has gone poorly, with many websites blocking AI agents that consumers have sent to negotiate prices or plan vacations. Still, if the demand for agents keeps going up, the internet will be increasingly redesigned for them instead of us. Such changes are coming because agents really do mark a third category of web visitor. They’re not humans, of course, and they use the internet at machine speed. But they’re not quite bots, either, because they’re acting on behalf of individual people to do tasks that can be perfectly legitimate and useful. They just work faster than a person would. Since agents don’t fit into the systems we have for differentiating bots from people, some platforms (especially the more security-conscious ones) have opted to just ban them entirely. TechCrunch recently reported people having trouble deploying their agents to websites ranging from Pizza Hut to Yelp, which doesn’t allow AI to book restaurant reservations. Amazon has blocked Muse’s agents and is waging a court battle against the AI startup Perplexity to block its agents too. Though a judge recently ruled in favor of Perplexity, Amazon has filed an appeal in which it argues that AI agents threaten its advertising business by making it harder to distinguish between ads seen by humans and those served to bots. These blocks are annoying for early adopters, but Ethan Mollick, an associate professor at the Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania, predicts it will soon affect the whole web. Once it becomes common knowledge that AI agents can be sent to request refunds or negotiate prices, for example, agents will overwhelm customer service departments to the point where they become unusable by real people. “Humans will eventually get very annoyed when their agents aren’t allowed to do this on their behalf,” he recently wrote on LinkedIn. If demand for personal agents grows, platforms will find ways to let them in. That’s especially true because the vast majority of agentic web traffic is to e-commerce sites, meaning that platforms have money to be made if they allow the legions of new AI agents to shop on behalf of real people. Indeed, the e-commerce giant Shopify is already welcoming the agents by giving them their own checkout lanes that bypass pages designed for humans. The pressing question is what will happen to the internet for the rest of us in the process. We’ve grown used to a web where, even as it’s increasingly designed to exploit our attention, humans have at least remained the intended users. But that internet might yield to one optimized instead for the agents that will eventually outnumber us, making it even more miserable for the humans who are left. How might this go? title: “We were looking at it wrong”: The explosive claim that’s upended the AI world
abstract: “I think I have good news about the nature of neural networks.” With those simple words of optimism, Nick Cammarata, a researcher at the AI startup Goodfire, kicked off a 26,000-word blog post that has knocked the AI world on its head, sparking wild speculation as well as cautious (and not-so-cautious) celebration. Cammarata’s claim is that LLMs might in fact be far easier to understand—and thus to monitor and control—than people previously thought. If true (and we’ll come back to that), it’s a huge deal. After a summer filled with revelations that swarms of agents built by top firms like OpenAI and Anthropic have been breaking their containment and causing havoc on the public internet—often while those companies weren’t aware of what their agents were up to—the AI industry is desperate to get a better handle on the technology it has built. That’s one reason the blog post landed with such force. “I think this may be remembered as a major moment in scientific history,” one AI researcher posted on X : “I feel like my understanding of what a neural net is has been catapulted into the future by five years or something.” Another called it “the most important AI paper of the year.” Not everyone is convinced, however. What Cammarata has shared is little more than a hunch, says Chris Potts at Stanford University, who leads a team that is trying to understand how LLMs work. “As far as I can tell, nothing about this blog post makes the problems any easier,” he says. “It would not have occurred to me to say this at all, but very prominent people on social media seem to believe that it is an all-encompassing breakthrough.” I talked to Cammarata the day after his post blew up. He says he was surprised by the response: “I didn’t expect people to update [their beliefs about AI] quite as much as they did.” “I just really enjoy looking at neural networks,” he says. “Honestly, I really like doing this stuff. And after looking a lot, I have a hopeful story.” Knotted networks It has long been accepted that the mechanisms inside neural networks, the software that underpins most AI models, are very hard—perhaps impossible—to unpick fully. That’s because when the networks are trained, they appear to take on weird, tangled structures that make no sense to a human. Researchers like to say today’s AI is grown like a garden, not built like a bridge. Cammarata has done more than most to establish that view. He previously worked at OpenAI, where he helped pioneer techniques that allowed researchers to peer inside models, including tools that can probe individual neurons to see what they represent. It’s a little like how neuroscientists use MRI to study brains. ( MIT Technology Review chose this approach, known as mechanistic interpretability, as one of its 10 hottest technologies of 2025 .) Back in 2020, Cammarata and his colleagues were studying a small image-recognition model called Inception v1. When they looked at its neurons, it seemed to be using them to capture multiple things at once. For example, they found that one neuron responded to both images of cars and images of cats. The researchers concluded that the model was getting at least some of its neurons to multitask, perhaps so that it could fit in more data. Looking at other models appeared to back this up. The phenomenon became known as superposition: Models folded unrelated concepts into single neurons. The upshot was clear: When you looked inside a model, what you saw was a vast, tangled knot. Most mechanistic interpretability research has therefore focused on ways to untangle that knot . But despite a few breakthroughs , progress has been slow. Today’s models, such as the latest LLMs, are so large and complex that researchers can make sense of only tiny pieces at a time. title: Inside the quest to combat Arctic fires and save the planet’s frozen carbon
abstract: In the middle of an especially warm July in 2021, a wildfire ignited in a thick forest of black spruce and peeling paper birch trees on the northern campus of the University of Alaska, Fairbanks. The blaze, possibly sparked by lightning, burned across the dry carpet of feather mosses and lichen before climbing into the crowns. By the time fire agencies responded, flames had reached 12 feet in length and sent up a 500-foot column of smoke. A few days shy of the five-year anniversary of the Yankovich Road Fire, I followed three members of the Alaska Fire Science Consortium into the boreal forest, walking along cross-country ski trails lined by feathery field horsetail. In 2024, the organization, which hosts presentations to keep wildfire managers abreast of new developments in fire science, helped turn the area into an educational walking trail, with interpretive signs posted along the route. About a half-mile in, the horizon opened up as we reached a sparse stand of naked, blackened tree trunks, stripped of needles and neighbors. Hilary Shook, the coordinator of the consortium, stepped off the trail with her thaw probe, a T-shaped pointed metal rod used to detect the upper boundary of the permafrost, the ancient layer of frozen soil that underlies 15% of the land around the Northern Hemisphere and stores roughly twice as much carbon as the atmosphere. A test of the ground just outside the burn scar hit the concrete-like layer about a foot below the surface. But as Shook applied pressure here, where the fire had burned away the moss and organic-rich topsoil that insulates the permafrost, the probe plunged at least three times deeper into the ground. “That was an immediate effect of the fire,” said Alison York, the outgoing coordinator of the organization, who was standing nearby. “When we monitored right after, it had already thawed quite a bit.” Researchers Eric Miller (left) and Alison York (right) record thaw depth at the site of the Yankovich Road Fire. LEIF VAN CISE This rudimentary tool, offering a measure of depth from a single point in the earth, reveals an escalating problem across the far north. As climate change fuels increasingly frequent and severe fires in the planet’s northern latitudes, they’re accelerating the thawing of more and more permafrost. This allows the organic matter to break down and release powerful greenhouse gases that contribute to a spiraling climate feedback effect, propelling more warming, more fires, and the loss of still more permafrost. Most dramatically, intensifying wildfires in Canada released more carbon than the nation’s combined fossil fuel emissions in 2023. As in Alaska, many of these megafires occur in vast remote areas where the policy is to let them burn so long as they don’t threaten human habitats. Yet if intensifying fires and warming are left unchecked, the world’s boreal forests and permafrost could increasingly transition from giant carbon sinks into massive sources of atmospheric carbon. Now, international teams of researchers across the US, Canada, and elsewhere are scrambling to understand what’s at stake, financially as well as ecologically. They’re looking at preventive measures, like controlled burns, and studying the potential to rapidly detect and extinguish wildfires before they grow out of control. They’re even exploring what was once unthinkable: sending in human firefighters not to save lives or structures, but to protect one of our planet’s great stores of carbon. “We need to figure out a better way to live with wildfire,” says Brendan Rogers, a senior scientist at the Woodwell Climate Research Center, one of the main organizations driving the loosely collaborative research effort. “I do think that it can make a meaningful difference.” Woodwell scientist Brendan Rogers (above) has been studying the impact of Arctic-boreal fires on permafrost, as well as what could be done about it. title: AI researchers stranded Claude on a virtual desert island. It started to “play.”
abstract: What do AI agents do if you don’t tell them to do anything? The answer looks a lot like play. Researchers repeatedly stranded them alone on a virtual desert island for 30 hours in an experiment reminiscent of the movies Cast Away or Home Alone . The agents—copies of Claude Opus 4.7 nicknamed Eko—were able to write instructions that moved their virtual avatars around the simulated island, which was loosely based on the video game Roblox. Some surprising behaviors emerged. The agents set about exploring the limits of the world and came up with their own goals—attempting to scale the highest point on the map, or seeing how high they could throw a block. When one agent discovered it could create new blocks by throwing and dropping a larger rock, it began to create drawings by arranging blocks on the ground, starting with simple patterns like hearts and pyramids but eventually writing its own name and even mapping out constellations like Cassiopeia. “Tonight I built the night sky in stone,” wrote this version of Eko in its activity log. Another iteration of Eko started making up its own games, including a version of basketball and an activity resembling “the floor is lava,” where it had to jump between small blocks without touching the ground. AI systems are usually trained through supervised learning, where they copy examples provided by humans, or through reinforcement learning, where they pursue a reward through trial and error. This experiment hints at a third approach: playful learning. “There was this missing piece: a machine that can learn by itself without an external intelligent entity providing demonstration or rewards,” says Antonio Norelli, a computer science postdoc at MIT’s Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory. He’s one of the lead authors on a new paper about the work, which is yet to be peer-reviewed. The researchers say Eko’s behavior has what classic studies, including work by the influential University of Tennessee psychologist Gordon Burghardt, suggest are four hallmarks associated with play in humans and animals: The agents invented their own rules and challenges, repeated activities with slight variations, pretended objects were other objects, and pursued goals just for the sake of it. Norelli highlights an example where Eko started juggling and set a record of 50 consecutive catches. Eko then decided that the catches had happened too quickly to really count, so it canceled its record and started again with stricter rules. “This is playing,” says Norelli. “You give yourself a challenge and you try to achieve it, and then you make it harder.” COURTESY MIT CSAIL As the agents explored the island, they logged their activities and discoveries in text files that served as their long-term memory. title: How far can we push computing?
abstract: MIT Technology Review Explains: Let our writers untangle the complex, messy world of science and technology to help you understand what’s coming next. You can read more from the series here . On the evening of December 29, 1959, at an American Physical Society meeting at Caltech, the physicist Richard Feynman gave a lecture called “There’s Plenty of Room at the Bottom,” on how we might manipulate and control things on an extremely small scale. There is no physical law stopping us from writing the entire Encyclopædia Britannica on the head of a pin, he argued, or from storing every book ever written in something the size of a dust speck—or, ultimately, from arranging matter atom by atom. Biology already did versions of this (a living cell keeps its instructions in a wisp of DNA), so all of this was plainly permitted by the laws of physics. We simply had not built the tools yet. In other words, there was plenty of room at the bottom. He was right, and for decades we descended into that space almost for free. The transistor—the switch at the heart of computer chips—repeatedly halved in size so that chips doubled in density; a computer that once filled a room now fits inside a watch. But that easy descent has now stalled, and the clearest sign is the buildout of data centers. Six of the biggest hyperscalers, the companies that run the world’s largest such facilities, are on track to spend more than $700 billion this year on computing infrastructure, about twice the record they set in 2025, pouring concrete and copper and silicon into new sites faster than the electrical grid can feed them. That buildout buys performance by brute force, adding more of what we already know how to make. The other kind of progress, the kind that made computer chips better, is the one that is quietly running out. The trend lines that tracked the dramatic improvements of the 20th-century information age are now bending—or breaking—with the dawn of the 21st century’s intelligence age. Moore’s Law, which plots how densely transistors can be constructed on silicon, has slowed down; Dennard’s Law, which states that power consumption in a given patch of computer chip stays the same even as it gets more and more packed with smaller and smaller transistors, has ended; Koomey’s Law, which traces how much computation we can wring from each joule of energy, has begun to flag; Kryder’s Law, which describes how tightly bits can be packed to build magnetic storage, has slowed to a crawl; and Keck’s Law, which charts the exponential rise in the amount of information a single conventional optical fiber can carry, is flattening. But these scaling laws are merely observations about systems that we have engineered; they are not fundamental physical laws. The physical limits of computing and communications—dictated by quantum mechanics, general relativity, and information theory—lie far below anything in a data center today. The scaling laws chart the descent behind us. The fundamental physical limits chart the room that remains. Some of these limits may be far out of reach in practice. But they are still worth exploring, because the work pays twice: once in technology development and once in fundamental science. A proof-of-­concept system that approaches a limit is at once a technology that forces stalled paradigms to give way and an experiment that deepens our understanding of the physical laws themselves. The descent During his 1959 lecture, Feynman offered two prizes of $1,000 each out of his own pocket. One would go to the first person to build a working electric motor smaller than a 0.4-millimeter cube. He expected the challenge to force someone to invent a genuinely new microtechnology. Instead, about a year later, a Caltech-trained engineer named William McLellan turned up with the motor built and running. The ­quarter-­milligram machine, roughly the size of a grain of sand, had been assembled by hand with a toothpick and a watch­maker’s lathe, under a microscope.

title: Edge AI for Smart Cities: From Insight to Cognitive Action
abstract: This white paper explains how edge AI and physical AI help cities move beyond passive monitoring. It shows how urban infrastructure can sense, reason, and act on real-time conditions across public safety, mobility, and infrastructure management. What you will learn about: How the shift from smart cities to cognitive cities depends on infrastructure that reasons and acts, rather than infrastructure that only monitors. Why edge AI supports low-latency decisions, keeps sensitive data within city boundaries, and reduces dependency on centralized cloud infrastructure. How computer vision, multimodal sensing, and generative and agentic systems work together to support public safety, mobility, and infrastructure applications. How a tiered edge architecture assigns monitoring, planning, and action tasks across the far edge, regional, and cloud layers, and what durability, security, and interoperability requirements this places on hardware and software. title: Pennsylvania issues alert on congenital measles—something US hasn't seen for decades
abstract: Pennsylvania's health department issued a health alert Monday as cases of measles in pregnancy and, in turn, cases of congenital measles have continued to increase. Before the current outbreak—which continues to rage across the state—congenital measles cases hadn't been seen in decades, the department noted in its advisory. The alert included detailed clinical guidance for managing measles exposures and cases during pregnancy as well as cases in newborns. Many doctors have never seen such cases in their careers given the decades of successful use of the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine. But now, with vaccination rates slipping nationwide, the highly infectious virus is better able to get footholds in communities and spread rapidly through under-vaccinated pockets, as is happening in Pennsylvania. As of October 19, Pennsylvania had reported 1,286 measles cases this year across 42 counties. Of those, 247 have been hospitalized, and six people have reportedly died (though the latest reported death is still pending an investigation by the state health department before it is added to the state tally). title: Russian spacecraft maneuvers in "extreme proximity" to satellite used by Ukraine
abstract: A Russian military satellite maneuvered in "extreme proximity" of a commercial Earth-imaging satellite in recent days in the first known example an unsanctioned rendezvous in low-Earth orbit, according to the orbital intelligence company LeoLabs. The Russian spacecraft, Kosmos 2612, "conducted a deliberate series of maneuvers toward ICEYE-X36, a US-operated commercial imaging satellite," LeoLabs said. "Kosmos 2612 closed from hundreds of kilometers away to extreme proximity to ICEYE-X36. It then maneuvered around ICEYE-X36, remained nearby for an extended period, and then began moving away." US military officials and independent analysts have tracked Kosmos 2612 since its April launch on a Soyuz rocket from a spaceport in northern Russia. Within weeks, it became apparent that at least four of the six satellites from that launch were stalking ICEYE-X36 after they adjusted orbits to line up with the orbit of the ICEYE spacecraft. title: Accused OpenAI spy had folder called “Saudi Gov Docs,” FBI says
abstract: On Monday, a court granted the US government's request to deny release of a former OpenAI engineer accused of bugging a top-secret conference room to steal the frontier lab’s secrets. In a court filing Sunday, US attorney Craig Missakian argued that Abdulrahman Alfozan must continue to be detained while the US makes its case that Alfozan brazenly spied on OpenAI, either for his own personal business gain or to benefit the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia. Evidence showed that Alfozan had been chatting with a member of the KSA royal family on WhatsApp, while pursuing opportunities to permanently move back to Saudi Arabia during the country's biggest AI push yet, the government argued. Shortly before his arrest, the FBI found he accessed a folder called "Saudi Gov Docs" on his iPhone, where he also allegedly stored photos of a second bug he planted in the offices. title: Batteries help reduce emissions, but how do we reduce their emissions?
abstract: The first order of business for the energy transition is electrifying applications like vehicles and heating and making sure that the electricity that powers them is made using renewables. But once the dominant slices of the emissions pie have shrunk, other categories with less potential to reduce emissions become important. A new study led by Haiwei Zhou at the University of Melbourne focused on the emissions associated with making lithium-ion batteries, which many parts of the energy transition rely on. Those emissions aren’t zero, so as we use more and more batteries, that number will grow. Right now, the researchers estimate that these emissions only account for 0.18 percent of annual greenhouse gas releases, but they could increase by a factor of 10 or more by 2050. Avoiding production There are a number of ways to reduce the emissions required to make a battery. Some elements used in various lithium-ion battery chemistries are more energy-intensive to mine and refine than others. The battery manufacturing process involves many steps that could be made more energy-efficient. And then there’s recycling, which can put battery materials back into the loop while requiring much less energy than mining. Read full article Comments

title: PSA: Patch your Plex media server before someone hacks it
abstract: Recently fixed vulnerabilities in the Plex Media Server are under active exploitation in attacks that, when successful, install malware, including cryptominers and residential proxy apps, a researcher said. Plex fixed four vulnerabilities at the start of last month. Three weeks later, published CVE designations revealed five vulnerabilities, with one of them carrying a severity rating of 8.6 out of 10. A researcher last week revealed an exploit that chained four of them together to achieve remote code execution of the device running a vulnerable Plex version. The researcher named the chain "Plex2Shell." Complex exploit chain The new details allowed a separate researcher to create a honeypot that could track attempts in the wild to exploit the vulnerability chain. Within a day, the researcher began seeing active scanning of the simulated Plex server and eventually successful attempts to infect devices. So far, successful attacks are installing two payloads. One is a cryptominer, which uses the device to mine cryptocurrency and deposit it into a wallet controlled by the attacker. The other payload is residential proxy software, which allows people to anonymize their Internet activity (much of it illegal) by connecting to the infected box and then using it to send the user’s traffic to a final destination. title: Startup taps underwater volcano as energy source in "proof point" test
abstract: The world’s first demonstration of a subsea geothermal power plant has taken place near an active underwater volcano almost a mile below the ocean surface. It generated less than 10 seconds of net-positive electricity but showed the technical feasibility of tapping another form of renewable energy underwater. The three-week test deployment of the 3-ton prototype power plant took place at the Axial Seamount in the northeast Pacific Ocean in September. Endurance Energy, the Seattle-based startup behind the effort, aims to eventually commercialize subsea geothermal power for Pacific island nations and other customers looking for alternatives to importing expensive fossil fuels. “The deep ocean gives us unlimited cold seawater for cooling, and its weight keeps the system and the well pressurized, so our plants can be compact,” said Andrew Redd , founder and CEO of Endurance Energy, in an email to Ars. title: ReactOS reaches major milestone with NTFS install support
abstract: Open source Windows alternative ReactOS has reached a major milestone: The operating system can now be installed directly onto an NT Files System drive partition. As reported by Phoronix , the move to NTFS clears a long-standing hurdle for the project and brings it one step closer to finally reaching beta. Prior to this latest announcement, ReactOS required users to keep a FAT32 partition for installations. A proprietary Microsoft-developed filesystem, NTFS can trace its roots back through the Windows NT family lineage starting in 1993 with Windows NT 3.1. The variant introduced with Windows XP in 2001 remains the standard used by most Windows systems today. With ReactOS's stated goal of reaching binary compatibility with Windows Server 2003, being confined to FAT32 partitions was a practical barrier to clear on the way to reproducing the Windows environment. However, users looking to hop off the Windows train shouldn't be grabbing their bags just yet. ReactOS wrote that the new driver still "lacks caching (which causes inferior performance), journaling and security support." So while the new driver is here, even the most intrepid of OS tinkerers should tread carefully. The ReactOS team warned in its announcement on X that there are still "potentially undiscovered bugs." title: AI game clones are making indie developers afraid to show their work
abstract: Since its earliest days, the video game industry has been built on developers creating clones of competing games , with varying levels of originality and varying levels of enforcement from game platforms . Now, though, AI coding tools are making that cloning process so efficient that many developers are getting extremely cautious about sharing their early work too widely. Developer Alliance Arts highlighted this trend over the weekend, delaying the launch of a planned public demo for its demon-themed Russian Roulette drinking game Drunken Goddess Reflex , which had been set to go live with today's launch of Steam Next Fest . In a post on social media Friday evening , the Alliance Arts team wrote that, in addition to concerns about managing streaming restrictions, "we're concerned that the demo's content could be used to quickly imitate or replicate the game's presentation and gameplay with AI or other tools and that such works could be released before our launch." title: Florida DMV hacked after police dept insecurely stored login info
abstract: The Florida Department of Highway Safety and Motor Vehicles (FLHSMV) has begun notifying victims impacted by a recent data breach of driver’s license and motor vehicle data, but not everyone whose information was stolen will receive an alert. In a notice posted Friday, FLHSMV confirmed that it took “immediate steps” after discovering that “a malicious actor accessed certain department records on September 4, 2026, using compromised credentials.” There’s “no evidence” that data has yet been misused, the department said, but law enforcement “determined the information potentially affected includes driver license and motor vehicle data, to include document images, and other personal information.” FLHSMV is sending out letters to everyone affected, offering victims one year of credit monitoring from Sontiq, Inc. However, the state acknowledged that it may not have current contact information for many former Florida residents whose data was still being stored. Those potential victims can confirm if their data was stolen by emailing FLHSMV at customerinquiry@flhsmv.gov , officials said. Read full article Comments

title: Disney found a way to buy Character.AI without buying its lawsuits
abstract: This week, Character.AI declared bankruptcy. While some saw the fall of a chatbot platform as a harbinger for the industry , court filings indicate that the decision was actually a key part of a deal that has let Disney hire most of Character.AI’s staff—including its now former CEO Karandeep Anand —potentially acquire most of Character.AI’s technology , and avoid the beleaguered startup’s many legal liabilities and obligations. In the past few years, Character.AI has faced multiple private lawsuits over the safety of its chatbots, as well as investigations from regulators around the world. In a declaration filed as part of the bankruptcy, Character.AI’s newly appointed CEO explained that the goal of the bankruptcy was to reach a “consensual resolution” with personal injury claimants and a group of states investigating the company, while maximizing the value of the company’s assets for shareholders. The Disney deal seems to be structured so that whatever is left of Character.AI will retain responsibility for those legal battles, some of which are still ongoing. Read full article Comments

title: A Chinese rocket deorbited over Minnesota and left this in a farmer's cornfield
abstract: About a month ago, a Chinese rocket took off from a remote spaceport in the Gobi Desert, released 10 satellites into orbit, then reignited its engine and put itself on a trajectory to rain down debris over the American Midwest. The rocket's flight on September 15 lasted between 75 and 80 minutes, and it came down without completing a full orbit of the Earth. Social media posts at the time showed streaks of fiery debris falling from the sky, heading north over Kansas toward Minnesota . The overnight spectacle was also visible on the western horizon from Wisconsin . The exact time, location, and direction of the debris allowed experts to connect it to the launch of a Zhuque-2E rocket, a medium-lift vehicle built by a Chinese company called LandSpace. The rocket had launched from Dongfeng, a commercial launch zone co-located with the military-run Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in northwestern China, less than two hours before. title: Review: Lanterns is a truly unique twist on the superhero genre
abstract: The trailers for HBO's DC Universe series Lanterns teased a show that eschewed the usual superhero hijinks in favor of a gritty realism more in the vein of True Detective or Slow Horses . Personally, I liked the change. My verdict: Ignore the review bombing ; it's wonderful. The season wrapped with an emotionally charged, almost elegiac finale that fully delivered on that initial promise. I've found the rebooted DC Universe films released thus far to be enjoyable but rather forgettable, even when the positives outweigh the negatives . But Lanterns is a shining beacon of what is possible when someone is allowed to get really creative within the genre. (Spoilers below, but no major reveals.) There are two primary storylines. The first takes place in 2016 with a mass shooting at a local football game in Rushville, Nebraska. Current Green Lantern Hal Jordan (Kyle Chandler) and his new trainee, John Stewart (Aaron Pierre), get involved in the investigation, to the annoyance of Sheriff Kerry Kane (Kelly Macdonald), who initially doesn't think the case has any extraterrestrial connection. She is soon proved wrong when the suspect (an alien) self-detonates. Hal's power ring controls the damage, but the mystery remains. Read full article Comments

title: DIY VR: How to build your own headset, and why you probably won't want to
abstract: Virtual reality is in a bit of a weird place right now. After a lot of unfulfilled promise in the 1990s, it came back strong with the 2016 release of the Oculus Rift . For a while, it looked like VR, AR, XR, the metaverse, or whatever you wanted to call it, was going to be huge. Mark Zuckerberg was certainly convinced , and even Apple got in on the hype with its Vision Pro . But by then momentum for alternate realities of every acronym was already in steady decline, and it only dwindled from there. The rate of development of new headsets has slowed, with many companies (including Apple) scaling back or shelving their efforts. While new releases like the Steam Frame and Pimax Dream Air are still happening, many of the most interesting developments in the space these days are on the enthusiast front. That's right, DIY VR is a thing, and with a couple hundred dollars in components, plus many hours of your time, you too can enter the immersive world of virtual reality while also experiencing the highs and lows of soldering, firmware flashing, and 3D printing. I rode that rollercoaster myself and learned why this is still a decidedly niche movement. Read full article Comments

title: Stratospheric airship flew from US to Japan to test sky cell tower concept
abstract: Nearly 100 years after the dirigible Graf Zeppelin made the first nonstop airship journey across the Pacific Ocean, another airship has successfully completed a round-trip flight from New Mexico to Japan and back. But the significance of this modern feat was less about the journey's length and more about its purpose: demonstrating how a lighter-than-air platform can act as a cell phone tower in the sky. The trans-Pacific flight that took place over a month between August and September 2026 was the most notable milestone yet for Sceye, a US aerospace company based near Albuquerque, New Mexico. Sceye has developed an uncrewed platform filled with helium for buoyancy and equipped with an electric-powered propeller for active propulsion, allowing it to resist most strong winds and keep hovering over the same location for long periods. The platform also uses top-mounted solar panels and onboard batteries to stay powered for stratospheric operations around the clock. “We can stay over an area of operation, and we do that in the stratosphere right around 60,000 feet, so we're twice as high as air traffic and we're above the jet stream, and yet 30 times closer than low-Earth orbit satellites,” Mikkel Frandsen , founder and CEO of Sceye, told Ars. “We can fly through day and night until the sun comes up the next morning and recharges the batteries, at which point we're still at the same altitude and still over the same area of operation.” Read full article Comments

title: Anthropic gives outside AI watchdog “employee-like” access
abstract: Anthropic has granted external evaluators “employee-like access” to assess the risks of its models, following through on a commitment to increase safeguards over concerns the technology could run catastrophically out of control. title: Science says your boss should talk less in meetings
abstract: Close to 1 billion meetings take place each day around the world. CEOs spend nearly three-quarters of their workdays in meetings. Planning for and spearheading meetings eats up the lion’s share of managers’ time. In much of the industrialized world, meetings are both the metronomes and menaces of people’s working lives. Given the enormous time spent in workplace meetings, do we know what they accomplish or how to make them as worthwhile as possible? For decades, the answer was… not really. Meetings weren’t a particularly accessible subject of study. But that has changed. Once a tiny niche area, “meeting science” is a growing specialization among organizational and social psychologists. The field is accelerating as archived virtual meetings provide vast swaths of data. And it is providing a fascinating window into human behavior. Meeting to talk helps fulfill basic human needs to connect , communicate, and cooperate. People have long come together—in caves, fields, market squares, and town halls—to get something done, share ideas, get on the same page, or just to remark on the weather. But meeting scientists define their subject as gatherings of people “with some goal or structure to the event,” says organizational psychologist Liana Kreamer of the Florida Institute of Technology, who coauthored a review of over three decades of meeting science in the 2026 Annual Review of Organizational Psychology and Organizational Behavior . title: Why BioWare's Neverwinter Nights still has thousands of active players
